label: Place
name: Andorra
summary:
Andorra, officially the Principality of Andorra, is a landlocked microstate in the eastern Pyrenees, bordered by France to the north and Spain to the south. With 77,000 people and 468 km² of territory, it is the sixth-smallest country in Europe and the largest of Europe's microstates. Andorra maintains a unique constitutional structure as a co-principality — ruled jointly by two co-princes: the Bishop of Urgell (in Spain) and the President of France.

Andorra's founding legend traces its independence to a charter of co-sovereignty granted by Charlemagne in 788 CE, though documented history begins with the 1278 Pareatge (treaty) between the Bishop of Urgell and the Count of Foix, formally establishing the co-principality. This medieval arrangement, survived intact through the French Revolution, the Napoleonic wars, and two world wars, making Andorra one of the world's oldest surviving constitutional arrangements — over 700 years of unbroken continuity.

Andorra remained a largely pastoral economy of shepherds and smugglers until the mid-20th century. The liberalization of trade and the development of duty-free retail and skiing resorts transformed it into one of Europe's most prosperous small economies (GDP per capita ranks among the highest in the world) and one of its most popular tourist destinations — over 10 million visitors per year to a country of 77,000 residents. It adopted a written constitution only in 1993 and joined the United Nations the same year. Andorra has no income tax, contributing to its role as an offshore financial center.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Andorra's unique co-principality structure has endured for over 900 years, with its medieval arrangement surviving intact through the French Revolution and remaining a model for modern microstates. The country's small size belies its significant regional impact as a buffer state between France and Spain.
